title: The third shock this hour
subtitle: A 67-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ICD, admitted to the CTICU after three appropriate shocks in an hour, now hemodynamically marginal.
objectives: Define electrical storm, state why the definition matters less than the trajectory, and list the reversible drivers that must be excluded in the first hour.
Explain the sympathetic-storm model and use it to justify beta blockade, sedation, and general anesthesia as antiarrhythmic therapy rather than as supportive care.
Choose between amiodarone, lidocaine, and procainamide for recurrent ischemic VT and state honestly what the evidence does and does not show.
Decide when a storm patient needs mechanical circulatory support, choose between Impella and VA ECMO with explicit reasoning, and explain why IABP is usually the wrong device.
Plan the anesthetic and ICU management of VT ablation on mechanical support, and name the bailout options when ablation fails.
Build an exit strategy after ablation that covers support weaning, ICD reprogramming, and advanced heart failure candidacy.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 67-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (remote anterior infarct, LVEF severely reduced on his last echo, a single-chamber ICD placed for primary prevention six years ago) is brought to the CTICU from the emergency department. He received three ICD shocks over the past hour, each preceded by palpitations and lightheadedness. The device was interrogated in the ED: each episode was monomorphic VT with a rate above the detection zone, antitachycardia pacing was attempted and failed each time, and each shock terminated the rhythm. [REVIEW]

He is awake, anxious, diaphoretic, and in sinus rhythm with frequent ventricular ectopy. Blood pressure is low-normal with a narrow pulse pressure. He is cool to the mid-forearm. Lactate is mildly elevated. Potassium and magnesium are at the low end of normal. Troponin is modestly elevated. The ECG in sinus rhythm shows his old anterior Q waves without new ST change. His home medications include a beta blocker, an ARNI, an MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor, and his wife mentions he was recently started on an antibiotic for a respiratory infection. [REVIEW]

An ED physician gave a single dose of IV amiodarone before transfer. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Does this patient meet the definition of electrical storm, and does it matter? Then list what you do in the first 30 minutes, with the device, the labs, the medication list, and the drug you reach for. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Definition.** The conventional definition, carried through the 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS and 2022 ESC ventricular arrhythmia guidelines, is three or more separate episodes of sustained VT or VF, or appropriate ICD therapies, within 24 hours, each separated by at least five minutes. [REVIEW] He meets it. The honest point is that the threshold is arbitrary. Three shocks in an hour in a patient who is cool and lactemic is a very different problem from three shocks spread across a day in a patient who is otherwise well. The definition gets him a label. The trajectory (rising frequency, failed ATP, hemodynamic deterioration between episodes) is what tells you how fast to move.

**The device.** Interrogate it yourself, or have EP do it at the bedside, and read the electrograms. Three questions: Are the shocks appropriate (true VT, not atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction or lead noise)? What is the VT cycle length, and is it slow enough that it could be reprogrammed into a zone where ATP has more chance of working? Is there a lead problem (impedance change, noise, oversensing) that is generating shocks for a rhythm that is not VT? In this case the ED interrogation says the rhythm is monomorphic VT and ATP failed. A reasonable reprogramming conversation with EP is to extend detection intervals and add further ATP attempts so that the device does less shocking for VT that is being tolerated. [REVIEW] A magnet placed over the generator suspends tachytherapies while leaving pacing intact. It is the right move if the shocks are inappropriate or if you are about to deliberately leave him in VT for an ablation or a reprogramming decision. It is the wrong move if the shocks are appropriate and life-saving and nobody is standing at the bedside with pads on. Keep external pads on him regardless. [REVIEW]

**Reversible drivers.** Ischemia first: the troponin is modestly elevated, which in a storm patient is usually demand or post-shock injury, but a new culprit lesion in a patient with coronary disease is the one cause you cannot afford to miss, so the question of angiography should be asked explicitly rather than deferred. [REVIEW] Electrolytes: replete potassium and magnesium toward the upper end of normal. The targets most storm reviews quote are expert opinion, not trial data. [REVIEW] Drugs: the antibiotic matters. A macrolide or fluoroquinolone prolongs the QT and, with amiodarone on board, is a reason to look hard at whether any of the episodes were polymorphic. [REVIEW] Stop anything QT-prolonging that is not essential. Check for thyroid disease, decompensated heart failure as the substrate, and device lead issues as above.

**The drug.** For monomorphic VT in a patient with scar, the 2022 ESC guideline and the 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline support IV amiodarone, with beta blockade as the second pillar. [REVIEW] Amiodarone has already been started. The addition that the data most favor is a non-selective beta blocker, because storm is in large part a sympathetic phenomenon: Nademanee and colleagues reported substantially lower one-week mortality with sympathetic blockade (left stellate ganglion block, esmolol, or propranolol) than with ACLS-guided antiarrhythmic therapy in post-infarction storm, and Chatzidou and colleagues reported that propranolol plus amiodarone terminated storm faster than metoprolol plus amiodarone. [VERIFY] [REVIEW] Lidocaine is the add-on if there is an ischemic component. Procainamide is the agent that PROCAMIO favored for tolerated wide-complex tachycardia, but it has a negative inotropic and hypotensive cost in a patient who is already marginal. [REVIEW]

**Sedation.** Treat anxiety and pain. Light sedation reduces sympathetic tone and is an antiarrhythmic intervention, not a comfort measure. Whether to go further, to intubation and general anesthesia, is the subject of the next stage. [REVIEW]

Specific amiodarone, lidocaine, and beta blocker doses are deliberately left out here. Insert the unit's dosing [NMH protocol, insert] and source any number to the guideline tables. [VERIFY]

questions.prompt: Single best answer. The ED gave amiodarone. He has another episode of monomorphic VT that ATP fails to terminate and that is shocked. His potassium and magnesium are now replete. Which single addition is best supported for reducing recurrence over the next hours: a second antiarrhythmic (lidocaine), a non-selective beta blocker, deep sedation and intubation, or immediate transfer for ablation?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: A non-selective beta blocker, with the explicit understanding that the choice is made on the sympathetic-storm logic, not on a definitive trial.** The reasoning is that recurrent monomorphic VT in an anxious, diaphoretic patient after multiple shocks is driven by scar substrate plus a sympathetic surge that each shock amplifies. Amiodarone addresses the substrate slowly. Beta blockade addresses the surge now. The Nademanee data and the propranolol-versus-metoprolol comparison both point toward sympatholysis as the intervention with a mortality or time-to-control signal. [VERIFY] [REVIEW] The cost is negative inotropy and bradycardia in a patient with a low pulse pressure, which is why it is done with the arterial line in, the pads on, and a plan for what happens if the pressure falls.

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **Lidocaine as a second antiarrhythmic.** Reasonable, and often done, especially if ischemia is suspected. The evidence for lidocaine in non-ischemic scar VT is weak and the evidence for stacking antiarrhythmics is weaker still. It does not address the sympathetic driver and it adds toxicity (neurotoxicity, further negative inotropy). It is a second-line addition, not the first.
- **Deep sedation and intubation now.** This is a real option and is where the case is heading. It is the step after beta blockade fails or cannot be given because of hypotension, because it carries its own costs (loss of the neurological exam, vasodilatation on induction, positive-pressure effects on a failing LV, the hazards of inducing anesthesia in a patient who may arrest on induction). In a patient who is still protecting his airway and talking, beta blockade comes first.
- **Immediate transfer for ablation.** Ablation is the definitive therapy for scar-related VT, but a patient who is cool and lactemic between episodes and has not yet been optimized medically is not the patient to put on the table tonight without support. The 2019 HRS consensus on VT ablation and the 2022 ESC guideline both frame ablation in storm as a recommended intervention when drugs fail, not as the first move. [REVIEW] It becomes the right answer in Stage 3.

The synthesis: beta blockade now, lidocaine if ischemia is suspected or beta blockade is not tolerated, sedation deepening in parallel, and the EP and MCS conversation started tonight even though the procedure is tomorrow.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
Six hours later. He has had four further episodes of monomorphic VT despite amiodarone infusion and a non-selective beta blocker. Two episodes were terminated by ATP after EP reprogrammed the device with longer detection and additional ATP sequences. Two required shocks. He is now intermittently confused. Between episodes the mean arterial pressure is low despite a low-dose vasopressor, the pulse pressure has narrowed further, urine output has fallen, and lactate has roughly doubled. [REVIEW]

Bedside echo: severely reduced LV function with a thinned, akinetic anterior wall and apex, mildly reduced RV function, no significant valvular disease, no pericardial effusion. [REVIEW]

Coronary angiography was performed between episodes: the old LAD occlusion is unchanged with collaterals, and there is no new culprit lesion. [REVIEW]

EP has reviewed the electrograms and the 12-lead of the clinical VT. They believe it is a scar-related reentrant circuit around the anterior infarct and are willing to ablate, but not tonight and not without support. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: He is deteriorating between episodes. Commit to the next two steps: what you do about sedation and the airway, and whether and which mechanical support you place now. Be explicit about why IABP, Impella, or VA ECMO.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Sedation and airway.** Intubate and anesthetize him. The indications are converging: he is confused, he is in low-output shock between episodes, and the sympathetic drive that each shock produces has not been controlled by beta blockade. General anesthesia blunts sympathetic outflow, removes the pain and terror of repeated conscious shocks, and allows the team to tolerate episodes of VT for a few seconds longer while ATP works rather than shocking immediately. The ESC guideline lists sedation and, if needed, anesthesia and ventilation as part of storm management, and case series report storm suppression with general anesthesia alone. [REVIEW] The choice of induction and maintenance agent is institution-specific and argued about. Propofol has vagotonic and sympatholytic properties and has been reported to suppress storm, but it is a vasodilator and negative inotrope at induction doses in a patient like this. Ketamine raises sympathetic tone and is a reasonable thing to avoid, although it is often chosen for induction in shock. Dexmedetomidine is attractive for sympatholysis once the airway is secured. No agent has been tested against another in storm. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW] The practical warning is that induction can itself precipitate VT or arrest, so this patient is induced with pads on, a vasopressor running, the EP team aware, and the support decision already made.

**Mechanical support.** Yes, and now. The reasoning is that he has cardiogenic shock between episodes, that the definitive therapy (ablation) is at least 12 to 24 hours away, and that the next episode may be the one that does not terminate. Support does three things: it maintains organ perfusion during VT so that the rhythm can be tolerated and mapped, it reduces the hemodynamic penalty of each episode so that the storm cycle (VT produces ischemia and sympathetic surge, which produces more VT) is broken, and it lets the team reduce vasopressors, which are themselves pro-arrhythmic. [REVIEW]

**Which device.**

- **IABP.** Usually wrong here. It is triggered off the ECG or the arterial waveform and loses effectiveness during rapid VT, which is exactly when support is needed. Its contribution to cardiac output is modest. It is the easiest device to place and may be the only one available at some centers, which is a reason to know its limitations rather than a reason to choose it. [REVIEW]
- **Impella.** A transvalvular LV pump maintains forward flow independent of rhythm, unloads the LV (which may itself be antiarrhythmic by reducing wall stress), and does not require an oxygenator or create retrograde aortic flow. Its limits in this patient: the RV is mildly reduced and VT with an unsupported RV can still produce collapse, the device produces electromagnetic interference with mapping systems, and it does not oxygenate. Impella CP flows are modest, and a larger device (5.5) is a surgical cutdown. [REVIEW]
- **VA ECMO.** Full biventricular support and oxygenation, rhythm-independent, and the configuration with the most published experience for supported VT ablation (Baratto and colleagues reported the Milan series of ECMO-supported unstable VT ablation). [REVIEW] Its costs are the ones covered elsewhere in this library: increased LV afterload and the risk of LV distension in a non-ejecting heart, North-South physiology if the lungs fail, bleeding, limb ischemia, and the need for a venting strategy if the LV stops ejecting. In a patient with biventricular dysfunction and shock who may spend hours in mapped VT, VA ECMO is the device most centers choose. [REVIEW]

**Commitment for this patient.** VA ECMO, peripheral, with a distal perfusion catheter, and a low threshold for adding an LV vent (Impella, ECPELLA) if the aortic valve stops opening or pulmonary edema develops. The reasoning is biventricular dysfunction, shock between episodes, the plan for prolonged mapping in VT tomorrow, and the possibility that this patient becomes a bridge to durable LVAD or transplant. The honest counterargument is that an Impella alone would spare him the afterload and cannulation costs of ECMO and that some high-volume EP centers prefer it. Which device NMH defaults to for storm is a local decision. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
He was intubated, anesthetized, and placed on peripheral VA ECMO overnight without incident. The storm quieted for several hours after cannulation, then resumed at a lower frequency, with VT episodes now tolerated hemodynamically on support and terminated by ATP in most cases. The aortic valve is opening on echo and the arterial trace is pulsatile. Lactate has normalized. He remains on amiodarone and the beta blocker. [REVIEW]

The EP team plans to ablate this afternoon in the EP laboratory with the patient on ECMO. The EP attending asks you to manage the anesthetic and the circuit in the lab. They expect a substrate-based ablation of the anterior scar and may also induce and map the clinical VT. They estimate four to six hours. They ask whether epicardial access might be needed, and whether you have a plan if the ablation fails. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Write the plan for taking this patient to the EP lab on VA ECMO: the anesthetic considerations, what changes about circuit management during the case, what you need from perfusion and EP before you leave the unit, and what you would do about the sedative and antiarrhythmic regimen in relation to inducibility.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Before leaving the unit.** The transport of a VA ECMO patient is the single highest-risk part of the day. Confirm the circuit (flow, sweep, oxygenator function with a post-oxygenator gas, cannula security, distal perfusion catheter flow), confirm the right radial arterial line is in and reading, confirm blood availability, and walk the route with perfusion. Agree on who manages the console in the lab and where they stand relative to the fluoroscopy arm. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Anesthetic.** The patient is already anesthetized and ventilated, so the question is not induction but maintenance. Three considerations are specific to supported VT ablation. First, inducibility: deep anesthesia, dexmedetomidine, and high-dose beta blockade suppress the arrhythmia the EP team is trying to map. The usual compromise is to continue the antiarrhythmics that have been working (stopping them risks an uncontrollable storm on the table and amiodarone would not wash out in time anyway), keep the beta blocker, and let EP use isoproterenol or programmed stimulation to induce if they cannot. Substrate-based ablation does not require the VT to be sustained. Discuss this explicitly with the EP attending before the case rather than discovering it at the first failed induction. [REVIEW] Second, the lungs on VA ECMO: keep the ventilator on lung-protective settings, do not assume the oxygenator will cover a lung that collapses on the table, and keep sampling the right radial gas because a recovering LV ejecting through atelectatic lungs is the North-South setup. [REVIEW] Third, positioning and access: the EP team needs femoral venous and often arterial access on a patient who already has two large cannulas in his groins. The cannulation plan the night before should have left them a side, and if epicardial access is being considered the subxiphoid route needs to be planned with the surgical team in the room or available, because a pericardial bleed on ECMO anticoagulation is a different emergency from one without. [REVIEW]

**Circuit management during the case.** Hours of induced VT with a non-ejecting LV is the setting for LV distension and thrombus. Watch the arterial pulsatility and the aortic valve on TEE or intracardiac echo. If the valve stops opening for a sustained period, the options are to reduce ECMO flow modestly if the hemodynamics permit, to add inotrope, or to vent (Impella or other). Decide the trigger for venting with perfusion and EP before the case starts. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW] Anticoagulation: EP ablation of the LV typically requires systemic heparin to a higher target than ECMO maintenance. Agree who owns the ACT and the targets. [NMH protocol, insert] Temperature management, pressor management, and fluid are standard but the retrograde ECMO flow changes how you interpret the arterial pressure during VT. Expect the mean to be maintained by the circuit even when the heart is doing nothing, and do not be reassured by it.

**Transfer back.** The same checklist in reverse, plus a post-procedure echo for new effusion, a lactate, and a limb check.

This is a four-way conversation (anesthesia, EP, perfusion, cardiac surgery) and the only part that is fixed is that it happens before the patient moves. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: The ablation runs five hours. The clinical VT is no longer inducible but a second, faster VT from the same scar remains inducible and EP cannot reach its exit. He returns to the ICU on ECMO. Over the next 12 hours he has two further episodes of the second VT. Rank the bailout options (stellate ganglion block, thoracic epidural, surgical cardiac sympathetic denervation, overdrive pacing, repeat ablation with epicardial access) and commit to one for tonight.
questions.modelAnswer:
**For tonight: a left stellate ganglion block, with overdrive pacing set up in parallel if the VT is slow enough to be paced out, and a repeat ablation discussion with EP in the morning.**

- **Stellate ganglion block.** Percutaneous, ultrasound-guided, performed at the bedside by an anesthesiologist, with onset in minutes and a duration of hours with bolus or longer with a catheter. The STAR study (Savastano and colleagues, 2024) reported that more than 90% of 131 patients with refractory storm had at least a 50% reduction in treated episodes in the 12 hours after the block, with few complications, and that a bolus plus infusion gave a longer effect than a bolus alone. [REVIEW] That is an observational series without a control arm, and the effect could be partly regression to the mean in a condition that waxes and wanes. The honest position is that the evidence is encouraging, mechanistically coherent, low-risk in the right hands, and not randomized. It is the right first bailout because it is fast, reversible, and does not require moving the patient. The risks (Horner syndrome, hoarseness, hematoma on anticoagulation, intravascular injection) are relevant on ECMO heparin and need a proceduralist who does this regularly. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]
- **Thoracic epidural.** The same sympatholytic logic at the T1 to T5 level, bilateral, continuous. The problem is the anticoagulated ECMO patient: a neuraxial catheter on therapeutic heparin is a bleeding risk most anesthesiologists will not accept. It is the better option in a patient who is not anticoagulated and not on support. [REVIEW]
- **Surgical cardiac sympathetic denervation.** Bilateral (or left-sided) thoracoscopic stellectomy and T2 to T4 sympathectomy. Vaseghi and colleagues reported durable reductions in ICD shocks and VT burden in a refractory population, with bilateral denervation more effective than left-only. [REVIEW] It is definitive rather than temporizing but requires an operating room, one-lung ventilation or a compromise on ECMO, and a thoracic surgeon. It is where this patient goes if the block works but does not last, and it can be combined with the surgical procedure if he goes on to a durable LVAD. [REVIEW]
- **Overdrive pacing.** Pacing faster than the VT, or faster than the sinus rate to suppress a bradycardia-dependent or pause-dependent trigger, through the ICD or a temporary wire. It is most useful for polymorphic VT and for slow monomorphic VT with a pause-dependent initiation. For a fast scar reentry it is unlikely to be the answer alone, but it costs little to set up. [REVIEW]
- **Repeat ablation with epicardial access.** The definitive answer if the second VT has an epicardial or intramural exit the endocardial approach could not reach. It is not tonight's answer because the patient has just had a five-hour procedure, the groin and pericardium need to recover, and the EP team needs to reassess the map. The morning conversation should be whether a second procedure, possibly epicardial, possibly with a different energy or a bipolar or needle approach, is realistic, and whether the better path is to stop chasing the substrate and go to a durable LVAD or transplant evaluation. [REVIEW]

The ranking depends on who is available at 2 a.m. and on the anticoagulation state. The order above is a defensible one, not the only one, and the ablation-first versus sympatholysis-first question is argued in the controversies section.

stages.title: The morning after
stages.narrative:
Day 4. The stellate ganglion block was placed with a catheter and the storm has been quiet for 30 hours. EP performed a second, shorter procedure with epicardial access and the second VT is no longer inducible. He remains on VA ECMO with a pulsatile arterial trace, an aortic valve that opens with every beat, and an LV that looks as poor as it did on admission. Lactate is normal. He is on a low-dose inotrope and no vasopressor. He has been lightened to the point of following commands. [REVIEW]

The attending asks you to plan the next 72 hours: how and when to wean the ECMO, what to do with the ICD before and after decannulation, and what the exit strategy is for a man whose heart was this poor before the storm started. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Lay out the weaning plan, the ICD programming plan, and the exit strategy. Name the question you would want answered by the advanced heart failure team before you decannulate.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Weaning.** The usual principles apply (the weaning literature is covered in its own case in this library): a stepwise reduction in flow under echo guidance with attention to LV outflow velocity, aortic valve opening, and filling pressures, with the sweep managed for the lungs separately. Two things are specific to storm. First, the wean itself is a sympathetic stress and a reduction in support, so it is the moment the storm may return. Keep the antiarrhythmic regimen and the beta blocker through the wean and do not perform it on the day the stellate catheter is removed. Second, a VT during a wean trial is an indication to stop the trial, not to shock and continue. If he storms on low flow, he is not ready to come off. [REVIEW] Timing: there is no evidence base for how long to wait after a successful ablation before weaning. Many centers want 24 to 48 hours of quiet rhythm at full support first. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**ICD programming.** Before decannulation the device should be reprogrammed from the storm settings (extended detection, multiple ATP sequences, possibly a monitor-only zone for slower VT) back to settings that will treat a recurrence without shocking him for every tolerated run. The decision belongs to EP, informed by what was ablated and what the residual inducible rhythms were. The ICU contribution is to make sure the reprogramming happens before he is awake and extubated rather than being discovered when he receives a shock on the ward, and to keep pads and a magnet at the bedside until it is done. If a magnet was used at any point, confirm the device is back in its normal mode. [REVIEW]

**Exit strategy.** This is the question that should have been raised on day 1. He has an LVEF that was severely reduced before the storm, he has now demonstrated that his substrate can storm despite amiodarone and beta blockade, and he has required mechanical support. He is, until proven otherwise, an advanced heart failure patient. The three exits are recovery to his prior baseline with ablation and drugs, bridge to durable LVAD, and bridge to transplant. The question for the advanced heart failure team before decannulation is: if he weans successfully but storms again in a month, is he a candidate for durable support or transplant, and if so, should he leave this admission with that evaluation complete rather than started? If the answer is that he is a candidate, the weaning strategy may change: some centers would take a patient like this directly from ECMO to a durable LVAD rather than wean to a recovery that will not last. If the answer is that he is not a candidate (age, comorbidity, frailty, preference), then the conversation is about what the ICD will do for him and whether he wants it to keep shocking him. That conversation is not an ICU afterthought. [REVIEW]

**The three questions to ask the attending at the end of this case** are whether this patient should have gone to ECMO at all or to an Impella, whether the stellate block was done too late, and whether the whole admission should have been framed as a durable LVAD evaluation from the first shock.

teachingPoints:
- Electrical storm is defined by a count (three or more episodes in 24 hours) but managed by trajectory. Rising frequency, failed ATP, and shock between episodes are the signals to escalate.
- The first hour is device interrogation (appropriate or not, lead problem, reprogrammable), reversible drivers (ischemia, potassium and magnesium, QT-prolonging drugs), and antiarrhythmic plus beta blocker. Keep pads on. A magnet suspends tachytherapy and is a tool, not a reflex.
- Storm is in large part a sympathetic disorder. Beta blockade, sedation, general anesthesia, stellate ganglion block, and surgical denervation are a single idea applied with increasing invasiveness. The evidence for sympatholysis is older and smaller than its place in practice, and should be presented that way.
- Amiodarone is the guideline default for scar VT. Lidocaine is an ischemic add-on. Procainamide performed better than amiodarone in PROCAMIO for tolerated wide-complex tachycardia but costs inotropy and pressure in a patient who is already marginal.
- Mechanical support in storm breaks the cycle of VT, ischemia, and sympathetic surge, and makes mapped ablation possible. IABP is rhythm-dependent and usually inadequate. Impella and VA ECMO are the real choices and the decision turns on RV function, oxygenation, access, and local expertise.
- Ablation on ECMO needs a four-way plan (anesthesia, EP, perfusion, surgery) covering inducibility versus suppression, LV distension during prolonged VT, anticoagulation ownership, and vascular access on a patient with two cannulas in his groins.
- Stellate ganglion block is fast, bedside, and supported by a large observational series. It is not randomized. Thoracic epidural is the same idea but rarely feasible on ECMO anticoagulation. Surgical denervation is the durable version.
- The exit strategy (recovery, durable LVAD, transplant, or palliation of a device that keeps shocking) should be named on day 1, not after decannulation.
pitfalls:
- Placing a magnet on a device that is delivering appropriate, life-saving shocks and walking away.
- Attributing an elevated troponin to the shocks without asking the angiography question explicitly.
- Stacking antiarrhythmics while leaving the sympathetic driver untreated.
- Inducing anesthesia for intubation in a storm patient without pads on, a vasopressor running, and the MCS decision already made.
- Choosing IABP for storm because it is the easiest device and discovering during the first VT episode that it has stopped augmenting.
- Stopping the antiarrhythmics before ablation to improve inducibility and producing an uncontrollable storm on the table.
- Letting the LV sit non-ejecting for hours during mapped VT on VA ECMO without a plan for venting.
- Weaning ECMO and removing the stellate catheter on the same day.
- Decannulating a patient whose ICD is still in its storm programming.
- Treating the admission as an arrhythmia problem and forgetting that a severely reduced LVEF that storms is an advanced heart failure referral.
controversies:
**Amiodarone versus lidocaine versus procainamide for ischemic VT.** The guidelines (2017 AHA/ACC/HRS, 2022 ESC) default to amiodarone for scar-related VT and list lidocaine for an ischemic component. PROCAMIO (Ortiz and colleagues, 2017) randomized tolerated wide-complex tachycardia and found fewer major adverse cardiac events and more terminations with procainamide than with amiodarone, but it was small, open-label, and enrolled hemodynamically tolerated patients, which this one is not. Some electrophysiologists read PROCAMIO as a reason to favor procainamide in the stable patient and amiodarone in the unstable one. Others point out that neither drug has good evidence in storm specifically and that the beta blocker is doing most of the work. [REVIEW]

**Early versus late ablation.** PARTITA (Della Bella and colleagues, 2022) randomized patients after a first ICD shock to immediate ablation versus deferral until storm and found lower death or heart failure hospitalization with immediate ablation in a very small randomized phase. VANISH2 (Sapp and colleagues, 2024) found first-line ablation superior to antiarrhythmic drugs for the composite of death, storm, shock, or treated VT in ischemic cardiomyopathy. Neither trial tells you whether to ablate in the first 24 hours of a storm or after medical stabilization. Expert practice has moved toward earlier ablation, but the patient who is in shock between episodes still generally gets stabilized and supported first. Where NMH draws the line is a local decision. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**The quality of evidence for stellate ganglion block.** The STAR study is the largest series and reports a striking response rate, but it is observational, multicenter, and without a control arm, in a condition that fluctuates. Older series and meta-analyses report similar effect sizes with the same limitations. A randomized trial (STAR 2) is registered. The honest framing is that the block is mechanistically coherent, low-risk in experienced hands, and widely adopted on evidence that would not be accepted for a drug. Whether it should be used earlier (before intubation and MCS, as some advocate) or reserved for refractory cases is unsettled. [REVIEW]

**ECMO versus Impella for storm.** VA ECMO has the largest published experience for supported ablation (Baratto and colleagues, 2016) and provides biventricular support and oxygenation. Impella avoids retrograde aortic flow and the afterload penalty, unloads the LV, and is preferred by some high-volume EP centers for patients with preserved RV function. There is no randomized comparison. The choice is usually made on RV function, oxygenation, access, expected duration of mapped VT, and which device the local team can troubleshoot at 2 a.m. The mapping-system interference from an Impella is real and manageable. [REVIEW]

**Anesthetic agent for storm.** Propofol, dexmedetomidine, and volatile agents have each been credited with storm suppression in case series. Ketamine is usually avoided for its sympathomimetic effect but is also the agent many would choose for induction in shock. None has been compared with another. [REVIEW]
discussWithAttending: The ED gave amiodarone. You added a beta blocker and he fell to a mean pressure that needed a vasopressor. Defend the beta blocker as the right call, then describe the patient in whom you would have withheld it and what you would have done instead.

Argue for an Impella alone instead of VA ECMO for this patient. What would have to be true about his RV, his lungs, and the EP plan for you to prefer it, and what is the failure mode you would be watching for?
The stellate block was done after intubation, ECMO, and a failed ablation. Make the case for doing it in the first hour, before any of that. Then explain why most centers do not.

EP wants him inducible. You want him not to storm on the table. Reconstruct the conversation you have before the case about antiarrhythmics, beta blockade, and anesthetic depth, and say where you would give ground.

He has an LVEF that was severely reduced before any of this. Was the correct plan from the first shock to treat this as a bridge to durable LVAD? What would have changed about the cannulation strategy, the ablation decision, and the conversation with his wife?
